Is that what to get on the ball means?
Hi, Anna. How has your day been?
I finished three reports and have only one more to do.
Wow. You are on the ball.
How did you do them so fast?
Coffee. Lots of coffee. Do you want some? I'll get it.
I'd love more coffee. Thank you.
Uh, sure. But maybe not that much coffee.
Someone who is on the ball finishes work quickly and ahead of time.
We can also say a person should get on the ball when they need to work faster or better.
And that's English in a Minute.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Hold Your Horses

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute.
Riding them takes skill and strength.
So, is the idiom hold your horses about controlling horses?
Oh, Andrew, can you help me with this box?
Just a second. I'm almost done.
Hold your horses is a way of telling someone to wait, to be patient.
And depending on how you say it, it could sound rude.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Strike a Chord

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute.
When you strike a chord in music, you play several notes at the same time.
So, are Anna and Andrew going to play music? I hope so.
I love Amelia Earhart. Her life really struck a chord with me.
Really? But she was a pilot, and you're afraid of flying.
Oh, no. Her flying career didn't strike a chord. She loved hot chocolate. And so do I.
When something strikes a chord with you, it causes strong reaction, usually because you identify with it.
Striking a chord can also mean that you're reminded of something familiar.

videos.title: English in a Minute: No Brainer

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute. We have to use our brains to think. So what does the expression
no-brainer mean? Hey, did you watch the new episode of Catch a Criminal? Yeah, but it was such a
no-brainer. The police found a gun and all the money in David's house. Well, what if David has a twin
brother who lives with him? The police would know if David had a twin brother. Well, what if they
don't know? Then they are really bad at their jobs. A no-brainer is something that requires little
thought or is obvious. It also means it is easy to make the right choice. And that's English in a Minute.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Stuck in a Rut

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute.
A rut in a dirt road can make wheels get stuck.
But what does it mean if a person is stuck in a rut?
Uh, Andrew, why are you wearing that wig?
I know, it looks funny, but I feel like I've been stuck in a rut.
I'm just trying to change things up and feel more creative and different.
I think it's just making my head hot.
To be stuck in a rut means you feel like you do the same thing over and over and need a change.
But maybe that is not the change Andrew needs.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Break the News

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute.
News can be any information that is, well, new to someone.
But what does it mean to break the news?
So, are you all ready for our big work trip to Brazil?
I just bought a new travel shirt, travel sunglasses, and this travel guidebook.
Andrew, I hate to break the news, but you're not traveling.
Budget cuts. There's not enough money for two.
But, can I borrow that travel book?
To break the news means to tell someone bad news, something that will make them upset or sad.
Breaking the news can be a hard thing to do, and so can hearing about it.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Head and Shoulders Above

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute. My shoulders and my head are both at the top of my body.
So what does it mean if something is head and shoulders above something else?
Andrew, I have found the perfect pizza. Perfect Pizza Palace!
That place is way too expensive.
Maybe, but their pizza is head and shoulders above all the other pizza places in this city.
And I have tried them all.
If something is head and shoulders above something else, it is better than all others.
It's as if it is placed higher than everything around it.
And that's English in a Minute.

videos.title: English in a Minute: Fair and Square

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute.
We all like to be treated fairly, but what about being treated squarely?
Let's learn how to use the idiom fair and square.
Anna, where have you been? I lost you in the crowd.
I was playing games. I'm really good at carnival games.
I see that. You really want a lot of stuffed animals.
Are you sure you didn't cheat?
No, I won them all fair and square, and they're all mine. All mine.
Fair and square describes winning something in an honest way and without any doubt.
The expression is a fun one to say because it rhymes. Fair and square.

videos.title: English in a Minute: The Bottom Line

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute. This piece of paper has lines at the top,
middle, and bottom. But what does the bottom line mean?
Andrew, did you watch the baseball game last night? Yes, I did. And I saw us lose
again. We need some new players. Well, they're getting better, and they tried
really hard. Yeah, they try hard, but the bottom line is you have to hit the ball
to win. They weren't hitting. The bottom line means the most basic or important
thing to consider in a situation. Bottom line can also be used to mean the
final result or outcome. And that's English in a Minute.

videos.title: English in a Minute: A Clean Slate

segs.text: Welcome to English in a Minute. In a classroom, the chalkboard is also called a slate.
It's important to clean it before starting a new lesson. So does clean slate relate to teaching?
I love the start of the new year. It's a great time to start fresh, make a new start.
Me too. This year, I'm going to start with a clean slate and give up bad habits.
Like eating donuts and drinking too much coffee?
A clean slate means a new start or beginning. This phrase comes from the use of chalk and slates in classrooms.
A teacher could start a new lesson with a clean slate.
And that's English in a Minute.
